title: The Train Ride Out of Birmingham to the Factory at Bournville
dek: In 1879 George and Richard Cadbury moved their cocoa works from a cramped city street into the fields, against the business opinion of the day.

story.event: Moving the cocoa works out of central Birmingham to a greenfield site at Bournville
story.summary: In 1878 the brothers George and Richard Cadbury, whose Bridge Street works in Birmingham had become too small, chose to build their new factory on the Bournbrook estate four miles south of the city instead of in its industrial districts, despite local business opinion that the move would fail. They arranged cheap rail tickets for their roughly 200 workers, built houses for foremen and sports grounds, and moved in the autumn of 1879; the factory had trebled by 1899 and George later built Bournville village around it.
paragraphs: In the autumn of 1879, as forewomen later told his daughter, Richard Cadbury went down to the old works in Bridge Street, Birmingham, and took a party of the factory girls out by train to their new workplace. He bought their tickets and pointed out landmarks as they neared the station. From the platform they walked up a lane to a factory standing in fields four miles south of the city, beside a trout stream called the Bourn.

Richard and his younger brother George had taken over their father's failing cocoa business in 1861 and very nearly closed it before it turned. By the late 1870s it was doing well, with about 200 workers, but Bridge Street was too small. They could have enlarged it or moved to the city's industrial quarter, as other firms did. George had watched gardens he remembered from boyhood turn into slums, and the brothers said that "our people spend the greatest part of their lives at their work".

In June 1878 they found the Bournbrook estate, about fourteen and a half acres beside a railway and a canal. Birmingham business opinion, George's biographer wrote, thought the plan an adventure without precedent that would end in disaster: the site was far from the city's labour and conveniences, and most workers would have to keep living in town. They had already given up trade for a principle, dropping their cheaper mixed cocoas after the food adulteration law of 1872. They went ahead, but met the objections one by one, negotiating cheap weekly rail tickets for their workers and freight rates as good as they had in town, and placing the factory on the part of the estate nearest the station.

Building began early in 1879. Bridge Street closed in July, after making enough stock to cover the move, and the workers arrived in September or October; accounts differ. They found a cricket and football field, a playground, dining rooms with a kitchen, and sixteen houses with gardens let to foremen at five shillings a week. The brothers said openly that such care also paid. By 1899 the factory had trebled in size and employed more than 2,600 people, and from 1895 George built a village nearby.

quote.text: Interest which is accused of all our misdeeds often should be praised for our good deeds.
quote.source_title: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims, tr. J. Hain Friswell, Project Gutenberg eBook #9105
quote.connection: The Cadburys are usually remembered for kindness, but they said the fields and the clean dining rooms were also good business, and an archive description notes that the wholesome image helped sell chocolate. La Rochefoucauld will not let either motive take all the credit, and the story does not need him to choose.

reflection: It is easy to feel that a good decision is spoiled if it also suits you. The Cadburys did not pretend otherwise. They believed healthier workers in pleasant surroundings would make a better business, said so, and the people on that train were still better off for it.

You will often act from mixed motives, and so will the colleagues you work beside. A more useful test than purity is whether the people affected are actually better off, and whether you are honest with yourself about why you chose it. The brothers also took seriously something simple: where people spend their working hours shapes their lives. That includes you.
invitation: Before you start work today, change one small thing about the place where you will spend most of the day, for no reason except that it will make the hours easier on you.

cross_checks.claim: In 1879 the Cadbury brothers moved their works out of central Birmingham to a country site four miles south, at Bournville
The estate was about fourteen and a half to fifteen acres, beside a railway and a canal
Business opinion expected the move to fail, and the brothers arranged cheap railway tickets for workers who still lived in the city
Building began early in 1879 and the workers moved in the autumn of 1879
The new works included sixteen houses with gardens for foremen and sports grounds
The move also served the firm's commercial interest, which the brothers acknowledged

research_notes: Workforce: the Cadbury World fact sheet says the workforce had risen to 200 and that the first trainload of 230 workers arrived in September 1879; Gardiner (1923) says the firm employed fewer than 300 hands. The story says 'about 200 workers'. Dates: Cadbury's own history says building began in January 1879; both Helen Cadbury Alexander (1906) and Gardiner say March 1879; the story says 'early in 1879'. Birmingham City Council and the fact sheet date the arrival to September 1879, Gardiner to October; the story gives both and says accounts differ. Acreage: 14.5 acres (Cadbury, fact sheet) against 'about fifteen acres' (Alexander, Gardiner); the story uses fourteen and a half. The brothers' statement about their workers appears in both books with one word different ('greatest part' in Alexander, 1906; 'greater part' in Gardiner, 1923); the story quotes Alexander. The scene on the train rests on forewomen's recollections recorded by Richard's daughter; she does not date it beyond the move itself. Cadbury's website attributes to George the remark about being content with a profit of a thousand pounds a year, while Gardiner attributes that sentiment to Richard; the story does not use it. Later village: the fact sheet says George bought 120 acres in 1895 and began building the village (other accounts date the land purchase to 1893); the story says 'from 1895'. The slate called the arc hard-responsibility; it is kept because the brothers framed the move as a duty to their workers and carried its risk, though it is also a change of site against convention. The archive.org text is OCR from the original editions; quoted words were checked against the scanned text.
